additions.reason: The 'previous days' (ימים הקודמים) are the experiential anchor of the teaching — the days when divine light shone upon the person. The text identifies these days with the sighted guide and with the staff that the blind man follows: they ARE the guide, they ARE the staff. This is a bechina: the previous days of illumination share the essential nature of the guide/staff — they orient the fallen person and show the direction. The text uses them interchangeably with the metaphor figures: 'יֵלֵךְ אַחֲרֵיהֶם' (follow them — the days) mirrors 'הוֹלְכִים אַחֲרָיו' (follow him — the guide).
additions.source_quote: צָרִיךְ לְחַזֵּק עַצְמוֹ בַּיָּמִים הַקּוֹדְמִים שֶׁהָיָה מַזְרִיחַ לוֹ אֵיזֶה הֶאָרָה קְצָת

additions.reason: The awakening of the heart (התעוררות הלב) and the shining/illumination (זריחה/הארה) are treated as a single compound reality in the text: 'הַהִתְעוֹרְרוּת וְהַזְּרִיחָה שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ אָז'. The conjunction 'וְ' (and) joins them as co-equal; they appear as two names for the same experience. This is a bechina: the awakening of the heart IS the illumination/shining. Both are the same spiritual state experienced from inside (heart-awakening) and from outside (light shining upon one).
additions.source_quote: וְיֵלֵךְ אַחַר הַהִתְעוֹרְרוּת וְהַזְּרִיחָה שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ אָז

additions.reason: The illumination (הארה) is paired with התעוררות as a co-equal name for the same experience. Additionally, the text ends with the same concept in a different form: 'יַחֲזֹר וְיִזְרַח לוֹ אוֹרוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ' (his divine light will shine again) — confirming that הארה/זריחה is the goal-state that the teaching aims to restore. The illumination IS the awakening; both belong in the same package as שמחה (the illuminated state IS the joyful state).

additions.reason: Falling from one's level (נפילה ממדרגה) is the opposing force in this Torah — the state that is the obstacle to joy and divine service. The text immediately introduces it as the challenge: 'אֲפִלּוּ אִם לִפְעָמִים נוֹפֵל מִמַּדְרֵגָתוֹ'. It is the condition of spiritual blindness ('נִסְתְּמוּ עֵינָיו וְלִבּוֹ'). In the teaching's good/evil mirror structure, this is the evil counterpart to Package 1's joy/illumination: the state of darkness that must be overcome.

The closed/blocked eyes and heart ('נִסְתְּמוּ עֵינָיו וְלִבּוֹ') are the experiential description of the fallen state — they are two names for the same spiritual darkness, joined as a compound. This is a bechina within the evil domain: the closed eyes ARE the closed heart, both being aspects of spiritual blindness. The text uses the blind man (סומא) analogy precisely because the fallen person is in this state. This node belongs in an evil/neutral package alongside נפילה ממדרגה.

analysis_notes.note_on_torah_structure: Torah #222 is a short practical teaching (3 sentences) with no explicit bechina language. Its structure is: (1) imperative (be in joy, serve God); (2) kal va-chomer analogy using blind man/guide/staff; (3) conclusion applying the analogy. The analogies use 'כמו שאנו רואים' (as we see) — kaf ha-dimyon, comparative language — not 'הוא בחינת' or other bechina markers. The blind man, the sighted guide, and the staff are rhetorical illustrations, not ontological identities. Consequently, no bechina edges exist in the dataset, and no packages can be built from the existing data. The concepts listed above are what would need to be added to the dataset as bechina edges before Torah #222 could be given packages.
analysis_notes.note_on_good_evil_mirror: If the Torah were populated with bechina edges, the mirror structure would be: Package 1 (שמחה / הארה / התעוררות — joy/illumination/awakening) as the good domain, mirrored by Package 2 (נפילה / עיניים ולב סתומים — falling/spiritual blindness) as the evil/opposing domain. The Torah's argument is entirely about restoring from Package 2 to Package 1 using the memory of past Package 1 states as guidance.
analysis_notes.note_on_analogy_vs_bechina: The staff (מקל) analogy deserves special attention. The blind man follows his staff because the staff orients him even when he cannot see. The teaching draws an explicit kal va-chomer: the blind man trusts his staff more than a blind man trusts a sighted guide — and 'how much more so' should a person trust his own past illuminated days. This suggests a functional identity: ימים הקודמים (previous days) ARE the staff/guide. However, this remains a rhetorical analogy (kaf ha-dimyon) rather than an explicit bechina. A dataset entry for this Torah would need to determine whether to encode this as a bechina (the days = the staff in essential nature) or leave it as eitza (the memory of past days functions as a guide — cause-and-effect).
